meta.nurseryNote: Nursery guides carry three things the others do not: the federal safety standard that applies, a prompt to check the model against the CPSC recall list, and a re-check schedule. That last one exists because every nursery manual we read says to inspect 'periodically' and none of them says how often or what to look at.

brands.name: IKEA
brands.system: Cam locks, wooden dowels, and on newer ranges a push-in wedge dowel that needs no tools. Allen key always included.
brands.tip: Every part has a number in the manual. IKEA ships replacement hardware free — search their site for 'spare parts'. Their manuals are pictures only, which is exactly why plain English helps.

brands.name: Sauder
brands.system: Their patented Quick-Lock system: a dowel-and-cam variant that pulls panels together with fewer separate pieces.
brands.tip: Sauder manuals number every part and their customer service ships missing hardware free. The back panels are thin — nail them properly.

brands.name: Zinus
brands.system: Steel frames with hex bolts and an included Allen key, plus foam mattresses in a box. Some frames fold out with no tools at all.
brands.tip: Zinus SmartBase frames need no tools: unfold, pop the legs out, done. Check which model you have before hunting for a hardware bag.

brands.name: Furinno
brands.system: Turn-N-Tube: plastic tube connectors you hand-twist together. No tools, no cam locks.
brands.tip: Hand-tighten only. These plastic connectors strip if you take a screwdriver to them.

brands.name: Ameriwood / Dorel / Novogratz / Mainstays
brands.system: Standard cam lock and dowel on laminated chipboard, plus metal-framed futons and beds.
brands.tip: Dorel brands share a parts service. Have the model number from the box end or the sticker inside the piece.

brands.name: Walker Edison
brands.system: Mixed metal and wood with hex bolts, often with a glass or slat shelf.
brands.tip: They publish assembly videos per product on their own site, which is worth a look alongside this guide.

brands.name: South Shore
brands.system: Cam locks, dowels and Confirmat screws — the fat ones that bite straight into chipboard.
brands.tip: Confirmat screws need to go in straight and stop when snug. Angling them splits the panel edge.

brands.name: SONGMICS / VASAGLE / FEANDREA
brands.system: Steel frame plus MDF panels, hex bolts, and a mallet in the box.
brands.tip: The included mallet is for the wooden dowels and panel joints, not the bolts. Use it where the manual shows a hammer icon.

brands.name: FlexiSpot / VIVO / UPLIFT
brands.system: Motorised standing desk frames with a control box and keypad.
brands.tip: A brand new frame that will not move almost always just needs the initialization reset: hold the down arrow for about ten seconds until it dips and beeps.

brands.name: Hbada / SIHOO / Furmax / Ticova
brands.system: Office chairs: star base, casters, gas cylinder, bolt-on back.
brands.tip: Gas cylinders are a near-universal size across brands. A failed one is a cheap part, not a dead chair.

brands.name: GTRACING / Dowinx / Homall / RESPAWN
brands.system: Racing-style gaming chairs with the back bolting to side brackets hidden under zipped flaps on the seat.
brands.tip: If you cannot find where the back attaches, open the zip or velcro flaps on both sides of the seat. The brackets are under there, often folded flat.

brands.name: Bestier / Rolanstar / Tribesigns / Cubiker / Armocity
brands.system: Metal frame desks and shelving with hex bolts, often with reversible left or right layouts.
brands.tip: These are usually reversible. Decide which side the long section or the shelf tower goes on before you tighten anything.

brands.name: Nathan James
brands.system: Metal frames with wood or fabric panels, hex bolts and washers throughout.
brands.tip: Their pieces lean on the washers to protect soft wood and fabric. Do not leave any out.

brands.name: Prepac
brands.system: Cam locks, dowels and a lot of back-panel nails. Often includes a hanging rail system for wall units.
brands.tip: Their wall-mounted pieces use a hanging rail that must hit studs. Measure the rail, not the cabinet, when marking the wall.

brands.name: Amazon Basics
brands.system: Varies widely by product. Steel bed frames with hex bolts, cam-lock cabinets, and tool-free wire shelving all appear under the same label.
brands.tip: Find the actual product type rather than searching the brand — the hardware differs completely between Amazon Basics lines.

brands.name: Costway / Giantex / Outsunny / HOMCOM / Best Choice Products / Devoko
brands.system: Outdoor and value furniture: bolts, nuts and washers rather than threaded inserts, so you often need a wrench as well as the Allen key.
brands.tip: Grease the bolt threads before assembly on anything that lives outside. It is the difference between a set you can repair and one you throw away.

brands.name: LUCID / Linenspa / Olee Sleep / Nectar / Novilla
brands.system: Mattresses and foundations in a box, vacuum compressed.
brands.tip: Unroll it flat on the bed frame before you cut the vacuum bag. And check your slat gaps — wide gaps are the real cause of most foam mattress sag complaints.

brands.name: Delta Children / Graco / Storkcraft / Dream On Me / Evolur
brands.system: Barrel nuts and long hex bolts, driven with a supplied M4 Allen wrench. A flat-head screwdriver is required to rotate the barrel nuts and is usually not supplied.
brands.tip: Manuals say explicitly not to use a power screwdriver — it strips the wood thread and snaps bolts. A flat-head screwdriver is needed to rotate the barrel nuts and is usually not in the box. Keep the booklet in the pouch sewn to the mattress support; you need it again at conversion time. These brands ship replacement crib hardware free — never substitute a hardware-store bolt.

brands.name: Babyletto / DaVinci / Namesake / Million Dollar Baby
brands.system: Same barrel-nut and hex-bolt system as the volume brands, usually on solid wood rather than engineered panels.
brands.tip: Conversion kits are sold separately and are model-specific. Buy the kit when you buy the crib — they get discontinued long before your toddler needs one.

brands.name: Graco / Chicco / Fisher-Price / Ingenuity / 4moms
brands.system: Tool-free folding gear: play yards, bassinets, high chairs and gates that lock by detent, over-center latch or threaded pressure cup.
brands.tip: With this category the question is almost never how to build it, it is whether every latch has actually locked. A click you did not hear is the failure.

terms.cam-lock: The small metal disc that drops into a round hole and twists to grab a bolt. Clockwise tightens. Counterclockwise releases it so you can take the joint apart.
terms.cam-bolt: A screw with a wide mushroom head that screws into a panel face so the cam lock can grab it. Tighten only until its shoulder touches the wood.
terms.dowel: A smooth wooden peg. It lines two panels up but holds no weight on its own. Tap it in to about half depth.
terms.square: Describes a frame whose corners are true right angles. You check it by measuring both diagonals: if the two numbers match, it is square.
terms.stud: The vertical timber inside a wall, usually every 16 or 24 inches. It is what you screw an anti-tip bracket into. Drywall alone will not hold furniture.
terms.anti-tip: A strap or bracket that ties furniture to the wall so it cannot fall forward. Required on anything taller than it is wide, and on every dresser in a home with children.
terms.washer: A flat metal ring that goes under a bolt head. It spreads the load so the bolt does not pull through the material. Never leave one out.
terms.shelf-pin: A small metal or plastic peg that an adjustable shelf rests on. Count holes from the bottom so all four pins are at identical heights.
terms.slat: One of the wooden boards that spans a bed frame to support the mattress. Gaps wider than about three inches will make a foam mattress sag.
terms.center-support: The bar running down the middle of a bed frame, head to foot, with its own legs. It carries most of the load and is not optional on a queen or larger.
terms.drawer-slide: The pair of metal runners a drawer rides on. They come handed, left and right, and must be mounted at identical heights.
terms.handed: Means a part exists as a mirror pair — a left one and a right one. Chair legs, drawer slides and sofa arms are commonly handed.
terms.gas-cylinder: The pneumatic post that raises and lowers a chair seat. Never cut or open one. When it fails the chair sinks, and it is a cheap universal replacement part.
terms.caster: A chair or cart wheel that pushes into a socket. No screws. Push until it clicks, and all of them should sit at the same height.
terms.mechanism: The tilt and height assembly bolted under a chair seat. The height lever goes on the right as you sit.
terms.stretcher: A bar between table or desk legs. It looks decorative but it is the brace that stops the piece racking.
terms.leveling-foot: A threaded foot you turn in or out to stop furniture rocking on an uneven floor.
terms.grommet: The plastic ring that lines a cable hole in a desktop.
terms.pilot-hole: A small hole drilled before a screw, so the screw bites instead of splitting the wood. Drill to about two thirds the screw length.
terms.threaded-insert: A metal sleeve set into wood that a bolt screws into. If one pulls loose, epoxy it back in and let it cure before bolting.
terms.barrel-nut: A metal cylinder that drops into a round hole in a crib or bed frame, with a threaded hole running across it. The bolt comes in from the side and threads into that cross hole. If the cylinder is rotated even slightly, the bolt cannot find the thread — turn the slot on its end with a flat-head screwdriver until you can see straight through it.
terms.confirmat: A fat, coarse-threaded screw that bites directly into chipboard with no cam needed. Drive it straight and stop when snug.
terms.tempered-glass: Heat-treated glass used in table tops. Strong on its faces, fragile at the edges, and it shatters all at once rather than cracking. Handle by the faces.
terms.initialization-reset: The procedure that re-zeroes a standing desk's motors: hold the down button for about ten seconds until the desk dips and beeps. Needed on every new desk.
terms.control-box: The electronics box under a standing desk that the motor, keypad and power cables all plug into.
terms.guard-rail: The barrier along a top bunk. Needed on both sides, including the wall side, and the gap above the mattress must meet the manual's minimum.
terms.plumb: Truly vertical. A gate that is not plumb will not latch reliably.
terms.off-gassing: The temporary smell from new foam. Harmless, and it fades in a day or two with the window open.
terms.bunkie-board: A thin solid platform that sits on a bed frame to support a foam mattress where the slat gaps are too wide.
terms.law-tag: The legal label sewn to a mattress. Photograph it — warranty claims need the model and date from it.
terms.glide: The plastic cap on a furniture leg. On outdoor furniture it also keeps water out of the hollow leg, which stops it splitting in winter.
terms.marine-grease: Water-resistant grease. A dab on each outdoor bolt thread at assembly means the bolts still undo years later.
terms.three-four-five: A way to check a right angle without a square: measure 3 along one side, 4 along the other, and the diagonal between those marks should be exactly 5. Works in any unit.
terms.corner-plate: The bracket under an L-desk that joins its two tops. Tighten this before the legs and work outward from it.
terms.connector: A plastic joining piece on tool-free furniture. Press it on square, fully home. Angled pressure cracks it.
terms.press-fit: A joint that holds by friction alone, with no screw. Push until it stops moving.
terms.sleeve: The two tapered plastic halves that clip around a wire-shelving post to make a collar for a shelf. Wide end up.
terms.wedge: How a wire shelf grips: its corner collar drives down onto the tapered sleeve and locks by friction.
terms.leg-plate: The metal plate that screws to a table or sofa underside and gives a leg something to thread into.
terms.clip-bracket: The hooked metal plate that joins two sofa sections. Lift one section slightly so the hooks can drop into each other.
terms.drawer-stop: A small clip that prevents a drawer pulling all the way out of the cabinet. Fit them — a loaded drawer coming out in your hands can pull a dresser over.
terms.hinge-adjust: The two or three screws on a cabinet hinge that move the door sideways, in and out, and up and down. Five minutes here is what makes doors line up.
terms.crossbar: The bar that joins two legs or two uprights. It looks decorative but it is the brace that stops the piece racking side to side. On a standing desk it also sets the desk's width.
terms.barrel-bolt: A long bolt used on beds and futons that threads into a cylindrical barrel nut dropped into a hole in the rail. Start it by hand — the barrel has to be rotated so its threads line up.
terms.mattress-support: The frame, springs or board that holds a crib mattress up, bolted at all four corners. It is the most repeated structural failure point in cribs, and because it sits under the mattress you never see it unless you look on purpose.
terms.two-finger-test: Push the mattress hard into one corner, then try to slide two flat adult fingers into the gap on the opposite side. If they fit easily, the mattress is too small for the frame. The most important five seconds in a nursery.
terms.slat-spacing: The gap between crib slats, which must be no more than 2 3/8 inches. A standard soda can is close to that width and will not pass between correctly spaced slats.
terms.preload: The clamping force a tightened bolt holds. CPSC testing found a crib fastener backed off as little as half a turn loses its preload, after which impact loading works it looser and opens a gap.
terms.five-point-harness: Two shoulder straps, two hip straps and a crotch strap meeting at one buckle. The crotch strap is the one that stops a child sliding down and out — without it you effectively have no restraint.
terms.submarining: When a child slides down and forward under a high chair tray instead of being held by the harness. It is the reason the tray is never a restraint.
terms.detent: The sprung catch that holds a folding joint in its open position. The click you hear is the detent seating. A joint that has not clicked can fold under load.
terms.over-center-latch: The latch used in play yard top rails. It locks by travelling slightly past straight, which is why the rail has to be pushed down and outward rather than just down.
terms.incline-limit: A bassinet sleep surface must sit at no more than 10 degrees. Steeper inclined sleepers are banned in the US after infant deaths. Flat is the target; 10 degrees is the legal ceiling.
terms.transit-lock: A bracket, bolt or tie fitted for shipping that stops a mechanism moving. Gliders and recliners commonly have one, and it must be removed before use.
terms.pinch-point: A place where a mechanism closes on itself. The scissor linkage under a glider is the classic nursery example and it closes with an adult's full weight behind it.
terms.stabilizer-bar: The bar fitted along the open side when a crib converts to a toddler bed. It does the structural job the removed side used to do and is not optional.
terms.toggle-anchor: A drywall fixing that opens out behind the board to spread the load. Far stronger than a conical plastic plug, and the right choice for anchoring furniture where there is no stud.
terms.pressure-mount: A gate held in place by friction from four threaded cups wound out against the frame. Acceptable in a doorway or at the bottom of stairs, never at the top.
terms.hardware-mount: A gate screwed into studs or solid timber. The only acceptable type at the top of a staircase.
terms.mesh-side: The fabric mesh wall of a play yard or travel crib. A tear in it is both an entrapment and a strangulation risk and ends the product's life.
terms.glide-mechanism: The linkage under a glider that converts the chair's motion into a smooth back-and-forth glide. It is also the pinch point.
